subject: Physics
title: Priya's Eye: How Light Bends
hook: Priya's glasses have stopped working. To get them fixed, she must understand why lenses bend light and how her eye focuses.

slides.title: Ray Optics and Optical Instruments: Seeing the World Clearly
slides.storyContext: Priya's spectacles fog up as she enters the eye doctor's clinic on a humid Mumbai afternoon. Dr. Sharma hands her a pair of lenses. 'Before I give you new glasses, do you know how they work?' Priya shakes her head. 'Light bends when it passes through glass—refraction. Today, I'll teach you why, using nothing but geometry and one simple law.'

image.alt: Ray Optics and Optical Instruments: Seeing the World Clearly — Ray Optics and Optical Instruments

slides.title: The Mystery of Blurred Vision
slides.storyContext: Priya has worn glasses since class 8. Her friends tease her about 'four-eyes,' but she's learned to ignore them. At school today, a new experiment in physics class fascinates her: the teacher uses a convex lens to focus sunlight onto paper, burning a hole. 'That's the same lens,' the teacher says, 'that makes words in a book clear for myopic eyes.' Priya connects the dots: her lens bends light to form clear images on her retina. When the focusing isn't right, images blur. Dr. Sharma has challenged her: 'If you understand the math, I'll let you design your own lens strength.'

image.alt: The Mystery of Blurred Vision — Ray Optics and Optical Instruments

slides.title: Snell's Law & Refraction
slides.storyContext: Dr. Sharma dips a stick halfway into a glass of water at the clinic. 'Look, Priya, it appears bent even though the stick is straight. Light bends at boundaries between materials. This bending is refraction, and it obeys a simple law discovered 400 years ago.'

points.label: Snell's Law
points.text: n₁ sin(θ₁) = n₂ sin(θ₂), where n is the refractive index (measure of how much a material slows light), θ is the angle from the normal (perpendicular to the surface).

points.label: Refractive Index
points.text: n = c / v, where c = light speed in vacuum (3 × 10^8 m/s), v = light speed in medium. For air, n ≈ 1. For glass, n ≈ 1.5. Higher n means slower light, more bending.

points.label: Normal
points.text: The line perpendicular to the surface. Angles θ₁ and θ₂ are measured from the normal, not the surface.

example.problem: Light enters a glass lens (n = 1.5) from air (n = 1) at an angle of 30° from the normal. What is the angle of refraction in the glass?
example.solution: n_air × sin(θ_air) = n_glass × sin(θ_glass). 1 × sin(30°) = 1.5 × sin(θ_glass). 0.5 = 1.5 × sin(θ_glass). sin(θ_glass) = 1/3 ≈ 0.333. θ_glass ≈ 19.47°. The light bends toward the normal, bending closer to the vertical as it enters the denser medium.

slides.inSimpleWords: When light crosses from one material to another (like air to glass), it bends. The denser the material, the slower light travels in it, the more it bends.

image.alt: Snell's Law & Refraction — Ray Optics and Optical Instruments

slides.title: Thin Lens Equation & Magnification
slides.storyContext: Dr. Sharma shows Priya a diagram of a lens. 'A convex lens is like two refracting surfaces back-to-back. When parallel light rays hit it, they converge to a focus. For a thin lens, there's one beautiful formula that connects object distance, image distance, and focal length.'

points.label: Lens Equation
points.text: 1/f = 1/u + 1/v, where f is focal length, u is object distance (positive if real), v is image distance (positive if real, negative if virtual).

points.label: Focal Length
points.text: f is the distance from lens to the point where parallel rays converge (for convex) or appear to diverge from (for concave). Shorter f means stronger lens.

points.label: Magnification
points.text: m = v / (-u) = image height / object height. Positive m: upright. Negative m: inverted. |m| > 1: magnified. |m| < 1: diminished.

points.label: Sign Convention
points.text: Real objects/images (on standard side): positive distances. Virtual (on opposite side or behind mirror/lens): negative distances.

example.problem: A book is placed 20 cm from a converging lens with focal length f = 10 cm. Where is the image formed? Is it real or virtual? What is the magnification?
example.solution: 1/f = 1/u + 1/v. 1/10 = 1/20 + 1/v. 1/v = 1/10 - 1/20 = 1/20. v = 20 cm. Image is real (v > 0), formed 20 cm on the opposite side. m = -v/u = -20/20 = -1. Image is inverted, same size as object. This is the setup for a movie projector.

slides.inSimpleWords: A thin lens formula tells where an image forms based on how far the object is from the lens. The magnification tells if it's bigger, smaller, or the same size.

image.alt: Thin Lens Equation & Magnification — Ray Optics and Optical Instruments

slides.title: Optical Instruments: Eye & Microscope
slides.storyContext: Priya studies the anatomy chart on Dr. Sharma's wall. The eye is a marvel of optics: cornea and lens focus light onto the retina (like a camera sensor). 'Your myopia, Priya, means your eyeball is slightly too long or your lens too strong. Light focuses in front of the retina, and far objects blur. My glasses correct this by placing a diverging lens in front of your eye—it spreads the rays just enough so they refocus on the retina.'

points.label: Normal Eye (Emmetropia)
points.text: Relaxed: focal length matches eye length (~2.5 cm). Distant objects form sharp images on retina. Near point (closest focus): ~25 cm. Far point: infinity.

points.label: Myopia (Short-sightedness)
points.text: Eye too long or cornea too curved. Distant rays focus in front of retina. Correction: diverging lens (concave, negative f).

points.label: Hyperopia (Long-sightedness)
points.text: Eye too short. Rays would focus behind retina. Correction: converging lens (convex, positive f).

points.label: Microscope
points.text: Two converging lenses: objective (short f, near object) forms real magnified image; eyepiece (short f) acts as magnifying glass. Total magnification = m_obj × m_eye.

slides.inSimpleWords: The eye is an optical system that focuses light. Defects in focus cause myopia or hyperopia, corrected by lenses. A microscope uses two lenses to magnify tiny objects.

image.alt: Optical Instruments: Eye & Microscope — Ray Optics and Optical Instruments

slides.title: Mirrors: Reflection & Focal Length
slides.storyContext: Ramesh, Priya's classmate, shows her a curved mirror in the science lab. 'Reflection is simpler than refraction,' he says. 'Light bounces off a mirror following one rule: angle of incidence equals angle of reflection. But a curved mirror focuses light like a lens does.'

points.label: Law of Reflection
points.text: θ_incident = θ_reflected, both measured from the normal to the surface.

points.label: Concave Mirror (Converging)
points.text: Reflects light toward a focus. Focal length f is positive. Mirror equation: same as lens, 1/f = 1/u + 1/v.

points.label: Convex Mirror (Diverging)
points.text: Reflects light away from focus. Focal length f is negative. Used for wide-angle rear-view mirrors.

points.label: Focal Length of Curved Mirror
points.text: f = R / 2, where R is radius of curvature.

example.problem: An object is placed 30 cm from a concave mirror with focal length f = 10 cm. Find the image position, nature, and magnification.
example.solution: 1/f = 1/u + 1/v. 1/10 = 1/30 + 1/v. 1/v = 1/10 - 1/30 = 2/30 = 1/15. v = 15 cm. Image is real, inverted, formed 15 cm in front of mirror. m = -v/u = -15/30 = -0.5. Image is half the size (diminished) and inverted. This is used in makeup mirrors and searchlights.

slides.inSimpleWords: Curved mirrors focus light via reflection, following the same mirror equation as lenses. Concave mirrors converge; convex mirrors diverge.

image.alt: Mirrors: Reflection & Focal Length — Ray Optics and Optical Instruments

slides.title: Worked Example: Telescope Design
slides.storyContext: Priya visits a planetarium in her city and sees the telescope. 'How do astronomers see so far into space?' she wonders. An enthusiast explains: 'A telescope also uses two lenses—exactly like a microscope, but arranged for distant objects. The objective collects faint light from stars, and the eyepiece magnifies. Let me show you the math.'

example.problem: A telescope has an objective lens with focal length f_obj = 100 cm and an eyepiece with focal length f_eye = 5 cm. (a) What is the angular magnification? (b) If the eye of an observer has a near point of 25 cm, what should be the tube length L (distance between lenses) for normal adjustment (image at infinity)?
example.solution: (a) Angular magnification M = f_obj / f_eye = 100 / 5 = 20. The telescope magnifies 20×. (b) For normal adjustment (relaxed eye viewing at infinity), the eyepiece forms a virtual image at infinity. This requires the intermediate real image from the objective to be at the focal point of the eyepiece. Tube length L = f_obj + f_eye = 100 + 5 = 105 cm. A 20× telescope needs a tube about 1 meter long.

image.alt: Worked Example: Telescope Design — Ray Optics and Optical Instruments

slides.title: Challenge: Designing Priya's New Glasses
slides.storyContext: Dr. Sharma gives Priya a project. 'Your near point is 40 cm instead of 25 cm due to myopia. I need to prescribe a lens such that you can read a book 25 cm away. The lens should also let you see distant objects clearly. What power (in diopters) do I need?'

example.problem: Priya's near point is 40 cm. She wants to read at 25 cm. She also needs to see distant objects. (a) What focal length lens corrects her vision for distance (infinity)? (b) For reading (25 cm), using the lens from part (a), where does the image form? (c) Power of lens in diopters: P = 1/f (in meters). Calculate P.
example.solution: (a) Myopia is corrected by a diverging lens (f < 0) that makes the infinity-image land on her retina. For a myopic person whose far point (unaided) is D_far (say 2 m), the correction is f = -D_far. Without knowing D_far precisely, we use: for myopia with near point 40 cm, a typical correction might be f ≈ -0.5 m to -0.67 m. Let's assume f = -0.5 m (example). (b) With the lens: using 1/f = 1/u + 1/v with u = -0.25 m (virtual object, since the book is now closer than the near point wants), 1/(-0.5) = 1/(-0.25) + 1/v gives 1/v = -2 + 4 = 2, so v = 0.5 m. But this requires careful refitting. (c) P = 1/|f| = 1/0.5 = 2 diopters (negative power: -2 D for a diverging lens).

image.alt: Challenge: Designing Priya's New Glasses — Ray Optics and Optical Instruments

slides.title: Recap: Ray Optics & Optical Instruments
slides.storyContext: Priya puts on her new glasses—crisp prescription, perfectly ground—and reads without strain for the first time in weeks. Dr. Sharma asks her to recap the lesson:

points.text: Snell's law: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂ governs refraction at material boundaries.
Thin lens equation: 1/f = 1/u + 1/v relates object distance, image distance, and focal length.
Magnification: m = -v/u tells us if images are magnified, diminished, upright, or inverted.
The human eye is an optical system; myopia and hyperopia are focusing errors, corrected by diverging and converging lenses.
Mirrors obey the same equation as lenses; concave mirrors converge, convex mirrors diverge.
Optical instruments (microscopes, telescopes, magnifying glasses) combine lenses to magnify objects.

image.alt: Recap: Ray Optics & Optical Instruments — Ray Optics and Optical Instruments

subject: Physics
title: Aditya's Interference Dream
hook: Aditya sees oil on a puddle shimmer with rainbow colors. His teacher reveals it's interference—proof that light is a wave.

slides.title: Wave Optics: Light as a Wave
slides.storyContext: Aditya notices an oil puddle outside his Mumbai coaching center, lit by morning sun. The surface is a kaleidoscope of reds, greens, violets. 'It's soap film interference,' says Prof. Nair, who happens to pass by. 'Two waves of light reflect off the top and bottom of the oil layer. Depending on the thickness, they can add up (bright) or cancel (dark). This is wave optics—where light shows its wave nature.'

image.alt: Wave Optics: Light as a Wave — Wave Optics

slides.title: Two Sides of Light
slides.storyContext: For centuries, Newton believed light was made of particles. But in class 12 physics, Aditya learns a shocking fact: light sometimes acts like particles (photons), sometimes like waves. Today's experiments use the wave model. Prof. Nair challenges him: 'If light is a wave, two light waves should interfere—they should add when in phase, cancel when out of phase. Find proof in the lab, and you'll have unlocked a secret Isaac Newton missed.'

image.alt: Two Sides of Light — Wave Optics

slides.title: Interference: Coherence & Path Difference
slides.storyContext: Leela sets up a ripple tank in the lab. Two dippers vibrate, creating waves that interact. 'See where the crests meet crests—constructive interference, big waves. Where crests meet troughs—destructive interference, calm water,' Leela explains. 'Light does the same. Two coherent light sources create an interference pattern.'

points.label: Constructive Interference
points.text: Path difference = nλ, where n = 0, 1, 2, ... Two waves crest-to-crest: amplitude adds. Intensity I = 4I₀ (for equal amplitudes).

points.label: Destructive Interference
points.text: Path difference = (2n+1)λ/2. Two waves crest-to-trough: amplitudes cancel. Intensity I = 0 (for equal amplitudes).

points.label: Coherence
points.text: For stable interference, sources must have same frequency (monochromatic) and constant phase relationship. Ordinary light sources are incoherent; lasers are coherent.

points.label: Condition for Visibility
points.text: Paths must differ by < coherence length (for light, ~few micrometers, thus need nearly monochromatic light).

example.problem: Two coherent light sources emit light of wavelength λ = 500 nm. At a point, the path difference is 1500 nm. Is it constructive or destructive interference?
example.solution: Path difference = 1500 nm = 3 × 500 nm = 3λ. Since 3 is an integer, this is constructive interference. Intensity is maximum.

slides.inSimpleWords: When two light waves overlap, they interfere: if crests align, they add (bright); if crest meets trough, they cancel (dark). This proves light is a wave.

image.alt: Interference: Coherence & Path Difference — Wave Optics

slides.title: Young's Double-Slit Experiment
slides.storyContext: Prof. Nair dims the lab lights and shows a classic setup: a laser, two slits cut in a screen, and a white wall beyond. A striped pattern of bright and dark lines appears. 'This is Young's experiment from 1801, Aditya. Monochromatic light passes through two slits. Each slit acts as a coherent source. On the wall, you see interference fringes. From the fringe spacing, we can measure the wavelength of light. Extraordinary.'

points.label: Setup
points.text: Light of wavelength λ from a source passes through two slits S₁, S₂ separated by distance d. Light is observed on a screen at distance D away (D >> d).

points.label: Path Difference
points.text: At a point P on screen, distance y from center: Δ = (d × y) / D (for small angles).

points.label: Bright Fringe
points.text: Δ = nλ. Spacing between adjacent bright fringes: Δy = λD / d. Smaller d or larger λ → wider fringes.

points.label: Dark Fringe
points.text: Δ = (n + 1/2)λ. Dark fringes are midway between bright fringes.

example.problem: In a double-slit setup, λ = 600 nm, d = 1 mm, D = 1 m. Find the distance between the central bright fringe (n=0) and the first bright fringe (n=1).
example.solution: Distance between adjacent bright fringes: Δy = λD / d = (600 × 10^-9 × 1) / (1 × 10^-3) = 0.6 × 10^-3 m = 0.6 mm. The first bright fringe is 0.6 mm from the center.

slides.inSimpleWords: Light passing through two slits creates an interference pattern of bright and dark lines. The fringe spacing reveals the wavelength of light.

image.alt: Young's Double-Slit Experiment — Wave Optics

slides.title: Diffraction: Light Bends Around Obstacles
slides.storyContext: Aditya looks at a light bulb through a fine-mesh cloth. The light spreads into a grid of bright and dark squares—diffraction. 'When light meets an obstacle or slit comparable to its wavelength, it bends around it. This is diffraction,' Leela explains. 'It's a consequence of wave nature. Particles don't diffract; waves do.'

points.label: Single-Slit Diffraction
points.text: Light passes through a single slit of width a. Waves from different parts of the slit interfere. Dark fringes appear at angles θ where a sin(θ) = nλ (n = 1, 2, 3, ...).

points.label: Central Maximum
points.text: Bright central fringe is twice as wide as side maxima. Most of diffracted light energy is here.

points.label: Intensity Pattern
points.text: I = I₀ [sin(β) / β]², where β = (πa sin θ) / λ. Maxima when β ≈ 1.43π, 2.46π, ...

points.label: Diffraction vs. Interference
points.text: Both are wave phenomena. Diffraction: single slit/obstacle. Interference: multiple coherent sources.

slides.inSimpleWords: When light passes through a narrow opening or around an obstacle, it bends and spreads. This diffraction is proof of light's wave nature.

image.alt: Diffraction: Light Bends Around Obstacles — Wave Optics

slides.title: Polarization & Optical Activity
slides.storyContext: Leela hands Aditya two pieces of polaroid film. When she stacks them, light passes through. When she rotates one 90°, darkness. 'Light waves oscillate perpendicular to their direction of travel. Normally, all directions are equal (unpolarized). Polaroid filters only allow oscillations along one axis. If two filters are perpendicular, no light gets through.'

points.label: Linear Polarization
points.text: E-field oscillates in one fixed plane. Polaroid filters absorb components perpendicular to their transmission axis.

points.label: Malus's Law
points.text: If light is polarized and passes through a polarizer, I_transmitted = I₀ cos²(θ), where θ is angle between polarization and polarizer axis.

points.label: Brewster's Angle
points.text: At angle θ_B = tan^(-1)(n₂/n₁), reflected light is fully polarized perpendicular to plane of incidence. tan(θ_B) = n_glass / n_air ≈ 1.5.

points.label: Optical Activity
points.text: Some substances (sugar, quartz, amino acids) rotate the plane of polarized light. Angle of rotation: θ = αℓ, where α is specific rotation, ℓ is path length.

slides.inSimpleWords: Light waves can be polarized (oscillations restricted to one direction). Polaroid filters, Brewster's angle reflection, and optically active substances demonstrate this.

image.alt: Polarization & Optical Activity — Wave Optics

slides.title: Worked Example: Measuring Wavelength with Diffraction Grating
slides.storyContext: In the advanced lab, Aditya uses a diffraction grating—a device with thousands of parallel slits. 'Each slit is a coherent source. The grating separates light by wavelength. Let me show you how to measure λ precisely.'

example.problem: Light passes through a diffraction grating with 1000 lines/mm. The first-order diffraction maximum (m=1) for a spectral line appears at an angle of 20°. Find the wavelength.
example.solution: Grating spacing: d = 1 / (1000 lines/mm) = 1 × 10^-6 m = 1 μm. Grating equation: d sin(θ) = mλ. For m=1, θ=20°: λ = d sin(20°) / 1 = 1 × 10^-6 × 0.342 ≈ 342 nm. This is in the ultraviolet range, suggesting this could be a cadmium or mercury spectral line.

image.alt: Worked Example: Measuring Wavelength with Diffraction Grating — Wave Optics

slides.title: Challenge: Oil Film Colors
slides.storyContext: Aditya returns to the puddle with oily film. 'Why are the colors arranged in rings and why do they change when I look from different angles?' Using thin-film interference, he works out the answer.

example.problem: A thin film of oil (refractive index n = 1.4) floats on water. Light of wavelength λ = 550 nm (in air, yellow-green) is incident normally. For constructive interference at the film surface (considering both reflections and phase change), what is the minimum thickness of the film?
example.solution: For a thin film with air above and water below: reflection at air-oil interface introduces a π phase shift (denser medium), reflection at oil-water interface has no π shift (less dense to more dense). Net phase difference from path = (2nt) × (2π/λ₀), where t is thickness, n is refractive index of oil. Adding the π shift from reflection: for constructive interference, 2nt = (m - 1/2)λ₀ (m = 1, 2, ...). Minimum: m = 1: t = λ₀ / (4n) = 550 × 10^-9 / (4 × 1.4) = 550 / 5600 × 10^-9 ≈ 98 nm. This is about 0.1 micrometers, confirmed by optical observations of oil films.

image.alt: Challenge: Oil Film Colors — Wave Optics

slides.title: Recap: Wave Optics
slides.storyContext: Aditya writes up his lab report. Prof. Nair reviews it with satisfaction. 'You've shown that light is truly a wave. The colors in soap films, the stripes in Young's double-slit, the spreading of light through a slit—all wave phenomena. Newton would be amazed.' Aditya smiles and closes his notebook:

points.text: Interference: Two coherent light waves add constructively (bright) or destructively (dark) depending on path difference.
Young's double-slit: Creates a striped pattern; fringe spacing β = λD/d reveals wavelength.
Diffraction: Light bends around obstacles or through slits; single slit produces dark fringes at a sin θ = nλ.
Polarization: Light's E-field can oscillate in a specific direction; polarizers, Brewster's angle, and optical activity show this.
Thin-film interference: Oil films, soap bubbles, and anti-reflection coatings use constructive/destructive interference.
Wave optics explains phenomena particle models cannot: Newton's rings, diffraction gratings, the photoelectric effect (partially).

image.alt: Recap: Wave Optics — Wave Optics

subject: Physics
chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
title: Rohan's Quantum Leap: When Light Behaves Like Particles
hook: Rohan's phone has a photoelectric cell. Pushing it toward a red lamp doesn't trigger it, but a blue lamp does. Why?

slides.title: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter: A Quantum Revolution
slides.storyContext: Rohan sits in Dr. Banerjee's quantum physics office, holding a smartphone with a broken camera sensor—it's being replaced because it's sensitive to only short-wavelength light (blue, UV) and not red. 'Your phone uses the photoelectric effect,' Dr. Banerjee explains. 'Light isn't just a wave; in 1905, Einstein showed it's also made of particles—photons. Each photon carries energy E = hf. Only photons energetic enough (high frequency) can knock electrons free from metal. Red light's photons are too weak. That's why your sensor fails with red light.'

image.alt: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter: A Quantum Revolution — Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter

slides.title: Particles of Light & the Photoelectric Mystery
slides.storyContext: For over a century, the wave model of light explained everything—interference, diffraction, polarization. But experiments in the early 1900s showed something strange: when light hits metal, electrons are ejected (photoelectric effect). The puzzle: no matter how bright red light is, it never ejects electrons. But even dim blue light ejects them instantly. 'This makes no sense,' Dr. Banerjee says, 'if light is purely a wave. Brighter light = more energy, so red should work.' Rohan gasps: 'Unless light is made of particles—photons—and each photon carries energy depending on frequency, not intensity.'

image.alt: Particles of Light & the Photoelectric Mystery — Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter

slides.title: Photon Energy & Einstein's Photoelectric Equation
slides.storyContext: Dr. Banerjee writes on the board: E = hf. 'Planck discovered this in 1900. h is a tiny constant (6.63 × 10^-34 J·s, Planck's constant). Higher frequency light = higher photon energy. A metal surface has a work function φ (minimum energy to eject an electron). If hf > φ, an electron escapes with kinetic energy KE_max = hf - φ. If hf < φ, no electron escapes, no matter how bright the light.'

points.label: Photon Energy
points.text: E = hf = hc/λ, where h = 6.63 × 10^-34 J·s, c = 3 × 10^8 m/s. Lower wavelength (higher frequency) = higher energy.

points.label: Work Function
points.text: φ is the binding energy of electrons to a metal (typically 2-5 eV for metals). Threshold frequency: f₀ = φ/h. Below this, no photoelectric effect.

points.label: Einstein's Photoelectric Equation
points.text: hf = φ + KE_max. Photon energy = work function + kinetic energy of ejected electron.

points.label: Stopping Potential
points.text: V_s = KE_max / e (in volts). A reverse voltage that stops even the fastest electron: eV_s = hf - φ.

example.problem: Zinc has a work function φ = 3.6 eV. Light of wavelength λ = 250 nm is incident. (a) Find the photon energy. (b) What is the maximum kinetic energy of ejected electrons? (c) What is the stopping potential?

slides.inSimpleWords: Light is made of photons, each carrying energy E = hf. The higher the frequency, the more energetic the photon. A photon hits metal and ejects an electron only if its energy exceeds the metal's work function.

image.alt: Photon Energy & Einstein's Photoelectric Equation — Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter

slides.title: De Broglie Waves: Matter as Waves
slides.storyContext: Zara, an artist, asks Dr. Banerjee: 'If light acts like matter (particles), can matter act like light (waves)?' Dr. Banerjee smiles. 'In 1924, Louis de Broglie proposed exactly that. Every particle—electron, proton, even a cricket ball—has an associated wavelength λ = h/p, where p is momentum. The more massive the object, the shorter its wavelength. Electrons are light enough that their de Broglie wavelength is measurable. This is why electrons can be diffracted, proving they're waves too.'

points.label: De Broglie Wavelength
points.text: λ = h/p = h/(mv), where m is mass, v is velocity, h = 6.63 × 10^-34 J·s. For non-relativistic particles.

points.label: Wavelength of an Electron
points.text: At 1 eV kinetic energy, λ ≈ 1.2 nm (in UV range, measurable with crystalline diffraction). At 100 eV, λ ≈ 0.12 nm (X-ray range).

points.label: Diffraction of Matter
points.text: Electrons, neutrons, and even atoms diffract through slits or off crystal planes, proving their wave nature. Used in electron microscopes.

points.label: Dual Nature
points.text: Photons and matter are both wave and particle: wave nature in propagation and interference; particle nature in energy and momentum exchanges.

example.problem: An electron is accelerated through a potential difference of 100 V. (a) Find its kinetic energy in eV. (b) Calculate its momentum. (c) Find its de Broglie wavelength.
example.solution: (a) KE = eV = 100 eV. (b) Momentum: KE = p²/(2m), so p = sqrt(2m × KE) = sqrt(2 × 9.11 × 10^-31 × 100 × 1.6 × 10^-19) = sqrt(2.9 × 10^-48) ≈ 5.4 × 10^-24 kg·m/s. (c) λ = h/p = (6.63 × 10^-34) / (5.4 × 10^-24) ≈ 1.23 × 10^-10 m = 0.123 nm. This is in the X-ray region, and matches experimental electron diffraction data.

slides.inSimpleWords: Electrons, like light, have a dual nature. They have a wavelength λ = h/p (de Broglie wavelength), which is why they can be diffracted and interfere like waves.

image.alt: De Broglie Waves: Matter as Waves — Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter

slides.title: Compton Effect: Photon-Electron Scattering
slides.storyContext: Dr. Banerjee describes an experiment: X-rays (high-frequency photons) scatter off electrons. The scattered X-rays have a slightly longer wavelength than the incident rays. 'This is impossible if photons are purely waves. But if photons are particles with momentum p = E/c = h/λ, then scattering is an elastic collision between a photon and an electron. The electron recoils, taking energy, so the photon exits with less energy and longer wavelength.'

points.label: Compton Scattering
points.text: High-frequency photon hits electron at rest. Electron recoils; photon scatters with reduced frequency (longer wavelength).

points.label: Wavelength Shift
points.text: Δλ = λ' - λ = (h/m_e c) (1 - cos θ), where θ is scattering angle, m_e is electron mass, h/m_e c ≈ 2.43 × 10^-12 m (Compton wavelength).

points.label: Compton Wavelength
points.text: λ_C = h/(m_e c) ≈ 2.43 pm (picometers). For 90° scattering, wavelength shift = λ_C.

points.label: Energy & Momentum Conservation
points.text: Before: photon E = hf, momentum p = E/c. After: photon E' = hf', electron KE and momentum. Totals conserved.

slides.inSimpleWords: When a photon collides with an electron, it scatters and loses energy, emerging with a longer wavelength (lower frequency). This proves photons carry momentum.

image.alt: Compton Effect: Photon-Electron Scattering — Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter

slides.title: Bohr Model & Quantized Energy Levels
slides.storyContext: Rohan asks: 'If electrons are waves, why don't they spiral into the nucleus? Why are atoms stable?' Dr. Banerjee explains: 'Niels Bohr in 1913 proposed that electrons orbit the nucleus in specific quantized orbits, where the electron's de Broglie wavelength fits perfectly around the orbit. An electron can only be in these allowed orbits; transitions between orbits emit or absorb photons of specific energies, producing spectral lines.'

points.label: Bohr's Quantization Condition
points.text: 2πr = nλ_dB = nh/(mv), where n = 1, 2, 3, ... Only certain radii are allowed.

points.label: Orbital Radius (Hydrogen)
points.text: r_n = (n²/Z) × a₀, where a₀ = 0.53 Å (Bohr radius), Z = atomic number. For hydrogen, r₁ = 0.53 Å, r₂ = 2.1 Å, etc.

points.label: Energy Levels (Hydrogen)
points.text: E_n = -13.6 eV / n². For n=1 (ground state), E₁ = -13.6 eV. For n=2, E₂ = -3.4 eV. E_∞ = 0 (ionized).

points.label: Photon Emission
points.text: Transition from n_i to n_f emits photon: hf = E_i - E_f = 13.6 (1/n_f² - 1/n_i²) eV.

example.problem: An electron in hydrogen jumps from n=2 to n=1 (Lyman alpha line). Find the energy and wavelength of the emitted photon.

slides.inSimpleWords: Electrons in atoms are confined to specific energy levels. They can jump between levels by absorbing or emitting photons. This explains atomic spectra.

slides.title: Worked Example: Photoelectric Effect Experiment
slides.storyContext: Rohan sets up a photoelectric experiment in the lab. He shines light of different wavelengths on a zinc plate and measures the stopping potential (reverse voltage that stops all photoelectrons).

example.problem: Light of wavelength 300 nm is incident on zinc (φ = 3.6 eV). (a) Is photoelectric effect observed? (b) If yes, find the stopping potential. (c) What is the threshold wavelength for zinc?
example.solution: (a) E_photon = hc/λ = (6.63 × 10^-34 × 3 × 10^8) / (300 × 10^-9) = 6.63 × 10^-19 J = 4.14 eV. Since 4.14 eV > 3.6 eV, yes, photoelectric effect occurs. (b) KE_max = 4.14 - 3.6 = 0.54 eV. Stopping potential V_s = 0.54 V. (c) Threshold: hf₀ = φ, so λ₀ = hc/φ = (6.63 × 10^-34 × 3 × 10^8) / (3.6 × 1.6 × 10^-19) = 3.45 × 10^-7 m = 345 nm. Light must be ≤ 345 nm.

image.alt: Worked Example: Photoelectric Effect Experiment — Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter

slides.title: Challenge: Electron Microscope Resolution
slides.storyContext: Rohan learns that an electron microscope can resolve features smaller than a light microscope. The reason: electron de Broglie wavelength is much shorter than visible light. A transmission electron microscope (TEM) operates at 100 kV. What is the electron wavelength, and how much better is the resolution?

example.problem: In a TEM, electrons are accelerated through 100 kV. (a) Find the kinetic energy in joules. (b) Calculate the momentum and de Broglie wavelength. (c) Compare to visible light (λ ≈ 500 nm). What is the improvement factor?
example.solution: (a) KE = eV = 100 × 10^3 × 1.6 × 10^-19 = 1.6 × 10^-14 J. (b) From KE = p²/(2m), p = sqrt(2 × 9.11 × 10^-31 × 1.6 × 10^-14) ≈ 5.4 × 10^-22 kg·m/s. λ = h/p = (6.63 × 10^-34) / (5.4 × 10^-22) ≈ 1.23 × 10^-12 m = 0.00123 nm. (c) Improvement: 500 nm / 0.00123 nm ≈ 4 × 10^5 times smaller wavelength. This allows resolution of atomic structures, impossible with light microscopy.

image.alt: Challenge: Electron Microscope Resolution — Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter

slides.title: Recap: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
slides.storyContext: Rohan closes his quantum notebook, understanding the revolution that reshaped physics. Light is not just waves; matter is not just particles. Both have dual nature, depending on the experiment. He tells Dr. Banerjee:

points.text: Light acts as particles (photons) with energy E = hf and momentum p = E/c.
Photoelectric effect: photons eject electrons from metal only if hf > φ (work function).
Matter acts as waves with de Broglie wavelength λ = h/p, allowing electrons to diffract and interfere.
Compton effect: photon-electron collisions conserve energy and momentum, confirming photon particle nature.
Bohr model: electrons are confined to quantized orbits where the de Broglie wavelength fits. Transitions emit/absorb photons with specific energies.
Dual nature is fundamental: the same entity behaves differently depending on how we measure it.
